candidateRows: Repeated hand copying before any surviving manuscript allowed errors to accumulate without a reliable means of reconstructing the earliest wording.
This transmission-history argument supplies the central reason for doubting that the original New Testament wording can always be recovered confidently.
Ehrman explains how copies of copies accumulated inherited and new mistakes, emphasizing that the originals and earliest generations of copies no longer survive.
The abundance of surviving New Testament manuscripts does not cure the absence of the early copies most needed to test the original wording.
It directly qualifies the common appeal to manuscript quantity by arguing that chronological proximity, rather than raw abundance, is the decisive evidentiary problem.
Ehrman acknowledges that New Testament copies greatly outnumber those of other ancient works, then stresses that most surviving copies are late and depend on unknown earlier exemplars.
The surviving manuscripts contain hundreds of thousands of variations, exceeding the number of words in the New Testament, while earlier variation remains unknowable.
The scale and uncounted early history of textual variation are offered as major evidence against complete confidence in recovering every original reading.
Ehrman recounts John Mill's thirty thousand noted variants, contrasts his hundred manuscripts with thousands now known, and says nobody can count all present or earlier differences.
Most manuscript differences are insignificant accidental errors that trained critics can usually identify, though some spelling variants can matter.
This concession narrows the dispute to consequential and difficult variants, preventing the raw variant total from bearing more argumentative weight than Ehrman claims for it.
Ehrman says most differences are misspellings, omissions, duplications, and similar accidental changes, and that trained readers can ordinarily detect them without difficulty.
The earliest Christian copyists were probably less trained than later monastic scribes, so the lost earliest period likely generated still more transmissional errors.
It shifts attention from detectable errors in surviving copies to potentially replicated errors arising before the surviving evidence, where direct verification is unavailable.
Ehrman contrasts literate medieval monastic copyists with largely untrained early Christian copyists and infers that early accidental mistakes were replicated into later manuscripts.
Some scribal changes appear intentional and important, while the absence of the earliest witnesses prevents knowing how many such changes occurred at the beginning.
The claim identifies consequential deliberate alteration and connects it to the evidentiary gap, supporting uncertainty about whether important original readings were preserved.
Ehrman distinguishes intentional changes from common accidental errors, acknowledges that scribal motives cannot be interviewed directly, and argues that the earliest period is unknowable.
The Trinitarian formula in First John 5:7–8 was not original despite its theological importance, illustrating a consequential later textual addition.
This concrete example demonstrates that a doctrinally prominent reading can enter the textual tradition and materially affect how readers understand a passage.
Ehrman describes the explicit Trinitarian wording found in the King James tradition, notes its limited Greek support and Latin history, and emphasizes its doctrinal importance.
Whether John 1:18 calls Jesus the unique God or the unique Son depends on which competing manuscript reading is accepted.
The example shows that a disputed textual reading can determine whether an important passage explicitly applies the designation God to Jesus.
Ehrman contrasts manuscript readings rendered as unique God and unique Son, arguing that the textual decision changes an explicit christological description in John's Gospel.
Luke's Gospel contains an explicit atonement formulation only if the longer disputed wording of Luke 22:19–20 is accepted as authentic.
The example ties a manuscript decision to whether an individual Gospel explicitly presents Jesus's death as being for others, making the variant interpretively consequential.
Ehrman notes Luke's omission of Mark's ransom saying and argues that the disputed longer Last Supper text supplies Luke's otherwise missing explicit doctrine of atonement.
The woman-taken-in-adultery narrative and Mark's longer ending are beloved but later additions absent from the earliest manuscript evidence.
These familiar examples support the claim that substantial and influential material could enter the tradition after the earliest recoverable textual stage.
Ehrman discusses the enduring popularity of the adulterous-woman story, its absence from early John manuscripts, and the snake-handling material in Mark's nonoriginal longer ending.
The real dispute concerns the significance of textual variants and the degree of confidence possible in recovering the original wording.
This passage directly defines Wallace's position on the debate motion and distinguishes recoverability from absolute certainty about particular readings.
Ehrman's contention that unresolved variants make the original wording unknowable and the text unreliable.
After identifying substantial common ground with Ehrman, Wallace isolates the parties' central disagreements and states his qualified confidence in textual recovery.
Scribal alteration did not erase the original wording, as identifying corruptions itself presupposes recoverable prior readings in the manuscript record.
The argument directly counters the possibility that early intentional alteration permanently removed the autographic wording from every surviving witness.
Ehrman's argument that uncontrolled early copying may have altered texts before the earliest surviving manuscripts.
Wallace invokes Ehrman's own scholarly identification of scribal tampering to argue that altered and prior readings remain distinguishable within the evidence.
The large raw number of variants is primarily a consequence of having many manuscripts, so that number alone does not show textual unreliability.
This argument reframes a principal quantitative basis for skepticism and connects abundant independent witnesses with increasingly secure textual reconstruction.
Ehrman's emphasis that surviving manuscripts contain more variants than the New Testament contains words.
Wallace defines textual variants, acknowledges estimates in the hundreds of thousands, and argues that additional manuscripts create both more variants and more checks.
The New Testament has unusually numerous early witnesses whose collective coverage compares favorably with the sparse remains of classical authors.
The dating and comparative abundance of witnesses directly support the claim that the New Testament wording is unusually well positioned for reconstruction.
Ehrman's claim that the chronological distance and scarcity of early copies prevent confident recovery.
Wallace counts witnesses within the first three centuries, notes their collective textual coverage, and contrasts them with the much thinner classical record.
Late New Testament manuscripts add relatively little material, while many classical works survive only partially and with much larger evidentiary gaps.
The comparison challenges the inference that late witnesses are worthless and argues that New Testament transmission is exceptionally complete by ancient standards.
The skeptical inference that predominantly late manuscripts are untrustworthy and leave the text no better preserved than other ancient literature.
Wallace contrasts limited accumulated additions and substantial early holdings with the incomplete, late, and sometimes conjecturally reconstructed remains of classical authors.
Applying radical doubt about the New Testament consistently to classical literature would undermine most knowledge of the ancient world.
It converts the comparative manuscript evidence into a direct defense of recoverability and rejects the variant-count argument as methodologically misleading.
Ehrman's conclusion that manuscript variation warrants saying there is no way to know whether the New Testament text is reliable.
Wallace characterizes the manuscript tradition as an abundance of evidence and argues that its variants and early witnesses enable reconstruction rather than defeat it.
More than ninety-nine percent of textual variants make virtually no difference because many involve spelling, word order, or untranslatable Greek forms.
This argument directly limits the significance of the headline variant total by showing that numerous formally different readings preserve the same meaning.
Ehrman's use of the enormous total number of manuscript differences as evidence against textual trustworthiness.
Wallace explains how Greek inflection, articles, word order, spelling, and conventional forms can generate many distinct readings with identical translation.
Fewer than one percent of variants are both meaningful and viable, although hundreds of genuinely disputed passages still affect interpretation.
The passage provides Wallace's principal quantitative qualification of significant variants while acknowledging unresolved cases rather than claiming complete certainty.
Ehrman's claim that intentional and consequential changes make important New Testament wording impossible to establish.
Wallace illustrates meaningful variants, summarizes their small proportion, and concedes that textual criticism still faces hundreds of interpretation-sensitive disputes.
No viable textual variant has been shown to jeopardize an essential Christian belief expressed in the New Testament.
The claim addresses whether consequential textual uncertainty undermines the doctrinal substance for which readers are asked to trust the New Testament.
Ehrman's examples suggesting that disputed or altered passages can materially affect significant Christian claims.
Wallace distinguishes interpretive disputes from threats to core doctrine and uses Ehrman's published formulation to support that narrower conclusion.
New Testament transmission is unlike a telephone game because written branches, earlier scribes, patristic testimony, and repeated access to originals preserve checks on copying.
The argument directly explains why missing first-generation copies do not entail cumulative unrecoverable corruption and supplies several mechanisms for reconstructing earlier wording.
Ehrman's emphasis that the originals, first copies, and several subsequent generations of copies no longer survive.
Wallace accepts the probable loss of early physical copies but argues that branching written transmission and independent historical witnesses prevent simple serial degradation.
The close agreement of Papyrus 75 and Codex Vaticanus preserves a textual tradition reaching back into the second century.
The relationship between two early, highly regarded manuscripts supplies affirmative historical evidence against wholesale early textual instability.
After arguing that Alexandrian copying was conscientiously controlled, Wallace uses two independent but closely agreeing witnesses to infer a much earlier common textual ancestor.
The standard critical Greek text indicates that the original wording survives among the manuscript variants in virtually every disputed place.
This directly supports recoverability by arguing that editors almost never regard the original wording as absent from all surviving readings.
Wallace contrasts tens of thousands of listed variants with only 116 places proposed as lacking an original Greek reading, noting that even those proposals were nearly all rejected.
Mainstream New Testament scholarship, including Ehrman's own substantive work, presupposes that the text has been recovered in nearly all essential and particular respects.
The argument uses ordinary scholarly practice as evidence that radical uncertainty about the New Testament's wording is inconsistent and unwarranted.
Ehrman's position that the unavailable earliest copies prevent confidence in the original wording.
Wallace cites Ehrman's authorship and vocabulary arguments as requiring stable textual wording, then concludes that substantial recovery is more reasonable than radical skepticism.
The abundance of later witnesses and the small percentage of extant meaningful variants do not answer what changes occurred before the earliest surviving manuscripts.
This isolates the central epistemic gap in the negative case: surviving witnesses cannot directly disclose editions, omissions, or alterations predating them.
Wallace's reliance on numerous manuscripts, patristic witnesses, and the low proportion of meaningful extant variants.
Ehrman accepts that numerous witnesses explain the large variant count but argues that this evidence is irrelevant to alterations made during the undocumented interval before extant copies.
Textual significance cannot be measured solely by doctrinal impact, and confidence is unjustified without evidence that the earliest surviving copies descend from accurate predecessors.
The move rejects a key criterion for minimizing variants and restates the decisive challenge concerning inaccessible, potentially significant early changes.
Wallace's claims that no essential Christian doctrine is affected and that the recoverable text can therefore be trusted.
Ehrman uses the hypothetical loss of entire biblical books to separate significance from doctrine, then demands a basis for treating extant manuscripts as copies of accurate copies.
Multiple early circulation, independent versions and patristic testimony, and high-quality early manuscripts provide cumulative probabilistic evidence for textual recovery.
This is Wallace's principal cumulative reply to the alleged evidentiary gap, combining dissemination history, independent witness streams, and scribal examples.
Ehrman's contention that no evidence establishes accurate transmission before the earliest surviving New Testament manuscripts.

Wallace argues that apostolic circulation and Gospel dependence imply repeated copying, that versions and patristic writers preserve early evidence, and that manuscripts such as P75 show meticulous transmission despite nonliterary hands.
Neither debater can know how often the earliest texts were copied or whether those copies were accurate, so later manuscript abundance does not establish the autographic wording.
The response directly denies that Wallace's probabilistic evidence bridges the undocumented transmission period and reinforces the negative burden concerning early accuracy.
Wallace's inference that early circulation, later manuscript comparison, and cumulative indirect evidence make accurate recovery probable.
Ehrman concedes ignorance about copying frequency, argues early scribes differ more and were less trained, and asks how unknown pre-survival variants can support trust in the text.

Textual criticism can reconstruct an exemplar through comparison even from error-filled descendant copies, and evidence suggests early Alexandrian differences are largely identifiable incidental errors.
The move explains the affirmative recovery mechanism and supplies an empirical analogy plus scholarly manuscript evidence against the inference from scribal mistakes to unrecoverability.
Ehrman's argument that increasingly poor early scribal performance leaves no evidential basis for reconstructing accurate predecessor texts.

Wallace concedes the lack of hard evidence but invokes cumulative probability, describes repeated reconstruction exercises, and distinguishes recoverable incidental variation from disabling textual chaos.
Contemporary textual critics reconstruct the earliest text ancestral to surviving witnesses, but cannot establish that this reconstructed initial text is the autograph.
This precisely defines the negative position's epistemic limit: successful reconstruction of an initial recoverable form does not prove identity with authorial wording.
Wallace's assertion that New Testament scholarship supports recovery of the original or autographic text.
Ehrman says major textual-research centers avoid the term original text and instead pursue the ancestral text behind surviving witnesses, whose autographic status remains unknown.
New Testament scholars' working assumptions and some textual critics' terminology still support substantial recovery, even when they avoid the phrase original text.
The exchange contests whether changed technical terminology reflects denial of autographic recovery or merely caution while retaining practical textual continuity.
Ehrman's claim that current textual critics reconstruct only an initial text and deliberately disclaim access to the autograph.

Wallace distinguishes New Testament scholars from textual critics, cites scholarly practice and named critics, while Ehrman counters that initial-text terminology exists because original identity cannot be known.
The initial text is not necessarily the original text, and scholars changed terminology because the autograph cannot be identified with certainty.
The distinction between an initial recoverable text and the author's autograph directly supports the con side's denial of autographic certainty.
Wallace's claim that current initial-text terminology still refers substantively to the original text.

After Wallace cites textual critics who still seek the original, Ehrman argues that institutional terminology changed precisely because the recovered initial text cannot simply be equated with the autograph.
Leading textual critics may avoid the phrase original text while still treating their reconstructed initial text as equivalent to what was formerly called the original.
This reply contests the con side's inference from changing terminology and defends substantive continuity in the discipline's reconstructive aim.
Ehrman's argument that abandoning the phrase original text shows scholars believe the autograph is unreachable.
Wallace responds that the cited institutional director and another textual critic use different terminology but continue to assume equivalence with the text once described as original.
Only extremely early, closely agreeing copies would provide strong evidence that a surviving text faithfully represents the original, and such evidence is absent.
The answer identifies the evidential condition Ehrman considers sufficient and emphasizes that the actual manuscript record does not satisfy it.
The questioner's suggestion that the existing manuscript evidence should already warrant describing the text as trustworthy.
Asked what evidence short of autographs would suffice, Ehrman imagines multiple copies made within a week of Mark that differ only minutely, then stresses that no such evidence exists.
Having more New Testament manuscripts than classical works makes reconstruction comparatively easier but does not establish possession of the original text.
This response directly rebuts a major comparative argument for trust by separating relative evidential abundance from successful recovery of an autograph.
Wallace's comparison claiming that the New Testament's superior manuscript abundance supports confidence beyond that afforded classical works.

Ehrman grants that the New Testament has far more witnesses than Homer, Plato, and other classics, but says classics also remain textually uncertain and that abundance alone does not yield an original.
Historical probability rules out total discontinuity with Mark but cannot determine how different the surviving Gospel is from what Mark originally wrote.
This closing formulation states the con side's core position: broad continuity may be probable while the degree and location of textual difference remain unknown.
Wallace's case that the surviving evidence permits sufficiently confident recovery and trust in the New Testament text.
Ehrman disclaims complete skepticism but argues that probability cannot establish exact recovery, citing the substantially longer form of Acts and acknowledged unresolved textual places.
The advocate of textual trust bears the burden of proving that the earliest copying was reliable, yet the quality of the first two centuries of transmission is unknown.
It supplies the con side's governing burden-of-proof argument and ties uncertainty directly to the poorly evidenced earliest phase of transmission.
Wallace's contention that the available manuscript tradition supplies enough probabilistic evidence for the text to be trusted.
Ehrman compares textual trust to sending a passenger train over a bridge, arguing that confidence requires evidence about early copyists and exemplars that the surviving record cannot provide.

Applying radical skepticism to the New Testament consistently would undermine knowledge of ancient literature generally, whereas historical inquiry properly relies on probability rather than certainty.
Wallace reframes the required standard of trust, arguing that demanding certainty would disable ordinary historical knowledge and that a moderate probabilistic standard is appropriate.
Ehrman's bridge analogy and claim that unknown early copying prevents the New Testament text from meeting the burden required for trust.

After briefly identifying Ehrman's final manuscript story as a hoax, Wallace answers the burden argument by locating all ancient texts on the same uncertain historical road and rejecting absolute skepticism.

Important variants can be recognized and matter historically without placing essential Christian teaching at risk, while the earliest recoverable wording remains accessible with substantial probability.
The move integrates acknowledged variants into the pro case by distinguishing meaningful local uncertainty from wholesale inability to recover or trust the text.
Ehrman's argument that unresolved variants and missing early evidence make the surviving New Testament insufficiently trustworthy.

Wallace cites the adulterous-woman story, Jesus' anger, and the later Trinitarian addition as consequential variants that critics can identify, then defends probabilistic recovery of earlier authorial wording.
Ehrman's own historical work presupposes detailed knowledge of authentic New Testament texts, which is inconsistent with portraying Wallace's probabilistic confidence as unwarranted certainty.
This consistency challenge uses Ehrman's reliance on authentic Pauline vocabulary and other textual judgments to support the practical recoverability defended by the pro side.
Ehrman's repeated characterization of Wallace's position as certainty and his own claim that the original wording remains fundamentally unknown.

Wallace says his confidence is relative rather than absolute and argues that Ehrman's books, including work distinguishing authentic Pauline letters, necessarily assume a reliable grasp of original wording.
